analysis.one_liner: Adds cost-benefit reviews and White House approvals that make federal regulations slower and harder to issue.
analysis.headline: Introduced in May 2023 with four Republican sponsors, the bill never received a committee hearing or a vote in either chamber before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite the basic process federal agencies use to write regulations. Every major rule would need review by a White House regulatory office before it could even be proposed, and agencies would generally have to adopt the option that costs regulated businesses the least, unless that office approved a different choice. Courts would get new power to second-guess agencies' legal interpretations, and agencies would be barred from encouraging the public to weigh in on proposed rules. The bill never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Regulated industries — manufacturers, energy producers, chemical and pharmaceutical companies, banks — would face fewer, slower, and easier-to-challenge federal rules, since agencies would have to pick the least-costly option for major rules and courts would review agency legal interpretations from scratch.

how_it_helps.text: For major rules, agencies would have to adopt the alternative that best minimizes costs to regulated entities, and could depart from it only with approval from the Administrator of the White House regulatory office.

Agencies would have to submit proposed major rules to the White House regulatory office for review before publication, publish an advance notice at least 90 days before a proposed rule, and give 90 days for public comment on major rules.
Courts would have to decide all questions of law 'de novo' — from scratch — rather than deferring to an agency's reading of its own rules, making rules easier to challenge in court.
Agencies would be barred from communicating with the public in a way that urges people to submit comments or advocate for or against a proposed rule, except for impartial requests for comment.
Agencies would have to publish assessment frameworks for major rules and periodically re-examine them to determine whether they should be modified or repealed.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people would wait longer for protections they already count on — clean air and water, workplace and product safety, drug and food safety, consumer financial protections — and would often get weaker versions, since agencies must generally choose the least-costly option and jump more procedural hurdles before a rule takes effect.
analysis.who_pays_short: Everyone relying on federal safety rules

drawbacks.text: An honest supporter would acknowledge the trade-off: cost-benefit discipline and mandatory consideration of alternatives could reduce rules that raise prices or impose burdens disproportionate to their benefits, which supporters say protects consumers and small businesses.
Some provisions are genuine transparency gains — agencies would have to place the studies and models behind a rule in a public docket and publish a plain-language summary of each final rule.

The bill would also exempt monetary policy by the Federal Reserve from all of its new procedures, and its ban on agency outreach would limit agencies' ability to alert affected communities that a rule is open for public comment.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The transparency provisions are real but modest next to the structural changes. The bill would put a procedural gauntlet in front of every major regulation — White House pre-clearance, advance notices, extended comment periods, a least-cost mandate, and easier court challenges — and the delay and weakening would fall mainly on the public's health, safety, and financial protections, while the savings accrue to the companies being regulated.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee in May 2023 and sat there with no hearing, markup, or vote until the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. James Lankford introduced the bill on May 16, 2023, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee.
Three Republican senators — John Thune, Ron Johnson, and Roger Marshall — cosponsored the bill; no Democrat did.
The committee took no further action: the record shows no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

The bill text would have required White House regulatory-office review before proposed major rules were published and would generally have required agencies to adopt the least-costly alternative for major rules.

It would have required courts to decide legal questions de novo, making agency rules easier to challenge, and would have barred agencies from communications urging the public to advocate for or against proposed rules.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained much — the bill simply died, and agencies kept their existing rulemaking procedures. Had it passed, regulated industries would have gained a slower, more litigation-prone process for every major federal rule, at the cost of delayed and weaker protections for the public.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Nothing changed; current rulemaking rules held

for.name: James Lankford
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it as its sole original sponsor.

against.name: Gary Peters
against.role: Chair, Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill as committee chair; it received no hearing or markup after referral and never advanced.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all three cosponsors were Republicans and no Democrat signed on; with no votes ever cast, the record shows the bill moving only through a committee chaired by a Democrat and then stalling.

industries.industry: Regulated industries (manufacturing, energy, chemicals, pharmaceuticals, finance)
industries.note: The bill would make every major federal rule slower to issue, weaker by default (least-cost mandate), and easier to attack in court. The savings from fewer or delayed rules go to regulated companies, while the public waits longer for the same health, safety, and consumer protections.

industries.industry: Consumer, labor, and environmental advocacy groups
industries.note: The procedural hurdles would delay rules these groups seek, and the ban on agency outreach would stop agencies from telling the public a proposed rule is open for comment — tilting the comment record toward well-resourced corporate commenters.

De novo judicial review of legal questions and added cost-benefit requirements would create more grounds to challenge rules in court and more analysis work, and the firms that profit from that work sit on the industry side of the line, not the public's.
